# tec

Tools to inspect python objects

To install:	`pip install tec`

# Examples

## Counting imported names

### Quickly (`tec.import_counting`)

`modules_imported` is a generator of module names from obj.
It uses string parsing, so is not as accurate as some other methods, but is fast and flexible,
and doesn’t require actually running any of the code analyzed.

```python
>>> from tec import modules_imported
>>> import os.path  # single module
>>> list(modules_imported(os.path))  # list of names in the order they were found
['os', 'sys', 'stat', 'genericpath', 'genericpath', 'pwd', 'pwd', 're', 're']
>>> import os  # package with several modules
>>> from collections import Counter
>>> Counter(modules_imported(os, only_base_name=True)).most_common()
[('nt', 5), ('posix', 4), ... ('warnings', 1), ('subprocess', 1)]
```

### Accurately (`tec.imports`)

When accuracy matters more than speed, `tec.imports` parses the code with the
standard library’s `ast`, so import-looking strings, comments and line
continuations can’t fool it. Each import comes back as an `ImportInfo`
(`name`, `filename`, `lineno`, `level`).

```python
>>> from tec import imports_in_code, count_imports
>>> [imp.name for imp in imports_in_code("import os\nfrom json import dumps")]
['os', 'json.dumps']
>>> count_imports(some_package_or_folder).most_common(3)
[('os', 12), ('dol', 7), ('re', 5)]
```

`count_imports` (and `imports_under_folder`) take a folder path, a module
object, a package, or an `__init__.py` path; what gets counted is decided by the
`import_key` argument, which defaults to the top-level package name.

> **Note.** `tec.imports` replaces `tec.findimports`, which held a vendored copy
> of the GPL-2.0-or-later `findimports` project – incompatible with `tec`’s own
> Apache-2.0 licence, and therefore removed. `tec.findimports` remains as a
> deprecated forwarding layer. The module-*graph* part of that old API has no `tec`
> equivalent; install the upstream project yourself if you need it.

## Modules

```pydocstring
>>> from tec import modules
>>> sorted(modules.second_party_names(modules))[:5]
['DOTPATH', 'FILEPATH', 'FOLDERPATH', 'LOADED', 'ModuleSpecKind']
>>> sorted(modules.second_party_names(modules, callable))[:4]
['ModuleSpecKind', 'coerce_module_spec', 'filepath_to_dotpath', 'finding_objects_of_module_with_given_methods']
>>> sorted(modules.second_party_names(modules, lambda obj: isinstance(obj, type)))
['ModuleSpecKind']
```

## Packages

A few functions to investigate what objects can be imported from a module
(and the depth of the dot-path to import those objects directly).

The main function, `print_top_level_diagnosis`,
prints a diagnosis of the imports that can be optained from the (top level) module.
That is, those objects that can by imported by doing:

```default
from module import obj
```

though the object’s code may be several package levels down (say module.sub1.sub2.obj).

```pydocstring
>> import numpy, pandas, scipy
>> print_top_level_diagnosis(numpy)
--------- numpy ---------
601 objects can be imported from top level numpy:
  20 modules
  300 functions
  104 types

depth	count
0	163
1	406
2	2
3	29
4	1

>> print_top_level_diagnosis(pandas)
--------- pandas ---------
115 objects can be imported from top level pandas:
  12 modules
  55 functions
  40 types

depth	count
0	12
3	37
4	65
5	1

>> print_top_level_diagnosis(scipy)
--------- scipy ---------
582 objects can be imported from top level scipy:
  9 modules
  412 functions
  96 types

depth	count
0	61
1	395
2	4
3	122
```

## Peek

```pydocstring
>>> from tec.peek import print_signature
>>> print_signature(print_signature)
func
sep: Union[str, NoneType] = '\\n'
prefix: str = ''
suffix: str = ''
>>> print_signature(print_signature, None)
(func, sep: Union[str, NoneType] = '\\n', prefix: str = '', suffix: str = '')
>>> print_signature(print_signature, '\\n * ', prefix=' * ', suffix='\\n')
 * func
 * sep: Union[str, NoneType] = '\\n'
 * prefix: str = ''
 * suffix: str = ''
<BLANKLINE>
```

# _autosummary/tec.dependencies.html.md

# tec.dependencies

Tools to analyze dependencies between python objects.

You may also wish to look at the unbox package for a more complete solution.

Packages to extract module dependencies are easy to find. Example:

* [https://github.com/thebjorn/pydeps](https://github.com/thebjorn/pydeps)
* [https://pypi.org/project/modulegraph/](https://pypi.org/project/modulegraph/)
* [https://pypi.org/project/findimports/](https://pypi.org/project/findimports/)

But to get this dependency analysis at a lower level is harder. There’s:

* [http://pycallgraph.slowchop.com/en/master/guide/index.html](http://pycallgraph.slowchop.com/en/master/guide/index.html)
  (but need to run the code – no static analysis that I can see)
* (There was snakefood, but no 3.x support !!!!)

I searched around AST and found some useful things there.
Often, around this AST code there are “fragility warnings” that say something along the
lines of “will not work in complex situations”.

My take on that is:

* if IDEs can refactor more or less correctly, then there’s a tool to do it sufficiently
* sufficiently is enough for most applications (it’s for the human, not the machine)

Gathered here are some tools to get the problem’s solution off the ground.

#### NOTE
The module requires `ast_scope` and `graphviz` to be installed.

### Functions

| `ast_scope_graph_to_dot`(ast_scope_graph)                                                    |                                                                    |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`dependency_graph_for`](_autosummary/tec.dependencies.html.md#tec.dependencies.dependency_graph_for)(obj[, prefix, suffix]) | Get graphviz Digraph object of the dependencies of a python object |
| `edges_to_dot_graph_edges`(edges)                                                            |                                                                    |
| `get_source_string`(obj)                                                                     |                                                                    |
| `source_string_to_ast_scope_graph`(source_string)                                            |                                                                    |
| `to_ast_scope_graph`(obj)                                                                    |                                                                    |

### tec.dependencies.dependency_graph_for(obj, prefix='rankdir="LR"', suffix='', \*\*digraph_kwargs)

Get graphviz Digraph object of the dependencies of a python object

# _autosummary/tec.findimports.html.md

# tec.findimports

Deprecated compatibility layer – use [`tec.imports`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#module-tec.imports) instead.

`tec` used to ship, under this module name, a vendored (lightly edited) copy of
the third party `findimports` project. That copy was distributed under the
GPL-2.0-or-later, which is incompatible with `tec`’s own Apache-2.0 terms, so it
has been removed.

What replaces it:

- Import finding is now done by [`tec.imports`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#module-tec.imports), an independent implementation
  written against the standard library’s `ast`. The functions of this module
  simply forward to it.
- The names that had no `tec` equivalent – essentially the module *graph*
  machinery (`ModuleGraph`, `ImportFinder`, `Module`, …) – are gone. If
  you need them, install the upstream project yourself
  (`pip install findimports`), keeping in mind that doing so subjects your work
  to *its* licence rather than `tec`’s.

Importing this module emits a `DeprecationWarning`. Asking it for one of the
removed names raises an `AttributeError` that says what to do instead:

```pycon
>>> import tec.findimports as fi
>>> fi.ModuleGraph
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
AttributeError: ...
```

### Module Attributes

| [`REPLACEMENT_MODULE`](_autosummary/tec.findimports.html.md#tec.findimports.REPLACEMENT_MODULE)          | Module that supersedes this one.                                                         |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`UPSTREAM_ONLY_ADVICE`](_autosummary/tec.findimports.html.md#tec.findimports.UPSTREAM_ONLY_ADVICE)        | Advice for the names that only the (GPL) upstream project provides.                      |
| [`REMOVED_NAMES`](_autosummary/tec.findimports.html.md#tec.findimports.REMOVED_NAMES)               | Names the removed vendored implementation used to provide, mapped to what to do instead. |
| [`REMOVED_NAME_ERROR_TEMPLATE`](_autosummary/tec.findimports.html.md#tec.findimports.REMOVED_NAME_ERROR_TEMPLATE) | Template of the error raised when a removed name is requested.                           |
| [`DEPRECATION_MESSAGE`](_autosummary/tec.findimports.html.md#tec.findimports.DEPRECATION_MESSAGE)         | Message of the `DeprecationWarning` emitted when this module is imported.                |

### Functions

| [`count_imports`](_autosummary/tec.findimports.html.md#tec.findimports.count_imports)(rootdir[, pathfilt, ...])   | Deprecated alias of [`tec.imports.count_imports()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.count_imports).               |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`re_find_imports`](_autosummary/tec.findimports.html.md#tec.findimports.re_find_imports)(rootdir[, pathfilt])      | Deprecated alias of [`tec.imports.imports_under_folder()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.imports_under_folder). |

### tec.findimports.count_imports(rootdir, pathfilt=<function \_is_py_path>, import_obj_func=<function base_package_of>)

Deprecated alias of [`tec.imports.count_imports()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.count_imports).

```pycon
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
...     _ = Path(root, 'a.py').write_text('import os.path\nimport json\n')
...     counts = count_imports(root)
>>> sorted(counts.items())
[('json', 1), ('os', 1)]
```

### tec.findimports.re_find_imports(rootdir, pathfilt=<function \_is_py_path>)

Deprecated alias of [`tec.imports.imports_under_folder()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.imports_under_folder).

Note the (harmless for the default) semantic difference: `pathfilt` is now
applied to store-relative paths, not to absolute ones.

```pycon
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
...     _ = Path(root, 'a.py').write_text('import os\n')
...     names = [imp.name for imp in re_find_imports(root)]
>>> names
['os']
```

### tec.import_counting.base_module_name(module_name_dot_path)

Base name of dot path module name

```pycon
>>> base_module_name('os.path.join')
'os'
```

Note that relative import names will resolve to an empty string.

```pycon
>>> base_module_name("..relatively_imported")
''
```

### tec.import_counting.imports_in_py_content(py_content)

Generator of imported names parsed out (with regex) of input code (string)

```pycon
>>> list(imports_in_py_content("import inspect ,  sys ;  import os.path\n  from collections.abc import Mapping"))
['inspect', 'sys', 'os.path', 'collections.abc']
```

### tec.import_counting.mk_multiple_package_import_regex(module_names)

Make a regular expression to parse out a specific modules names in the context of an import.

### tec.import_counting.mk_single_package_import_regex(module_name)

Make a regular expression to parse out a specific module name in the context of an import.

### tec.import_counting.modules_imported(obj, only_base_name=False, exclude_stdlib=False)

Generator of module names from obj.

#### NOTE
The process uses regular expressions to parse out imported names from string contents.
The process in by no means accurate in all cases.
It may have false positives (strings that have import patterns, but are not actual code imports).
It may have false negatives (relative imports (as in `..name`) and “dynamically” imported, etc.

If you need something more precise, use `tec.imports` (which parses the code with
`ast` instead of matching patterns), or look into other tools (snakefood, for example).

* **Parameters:**
  * **obj** – module object, file or folder path, or anything that can resolve to that
  * **only_base_name** – If True, will only return the first part of the dot names
* **Returns:**
  Generator of module (dot path) names

```pycon
>>> import os.path  # single module
>>> list(modules_imported(os.path))
['os', 'sys', 'stat', 'genericpath', 'genericpath', 'pwd', 'pwd', 're', 're']
>>> import os  # package with several modules
>>> from collections import Counter
>>> Counter(modules_imported(os, only_base_name=True)).most_common()
[('nt', 5), ('posix', 4), ... ('warnings', 1), ('subprocess', 1)]
```

### tec.import_counting.modules_imported_by_module(module)

Generator of module names that are imported in a module.

* **Parameters:**
  **module** – The module specification, which could be a filepath, the actual code (string) of the module,
  or any python object (module or object therein – that can be resolved by inspect.getfile(module))
* **Returns:**
  A generator of strings showing the imported module names (dot paths)

The input can be a filepath

```pycon
>>> sorted(modules_imported_by_module(__file__))
['collections', 'importlib.util', 'io', 'os', 'os.path', 'pathlib', 're', 'sys', 'sysconfig', 'tec.stores', 'tec.util']
```

… a imported module object

```pycon
>>> import wave
>>> sorted(modules_imported_by_module(wave))
['audioop', 'builtins', 'chunk', 'collections', 'struct', 'sys']
```

… the string contents themselves

### tec.import_counting.modules_imported_count(obj, only_base_name=False, exclude_stdlib=False)

A dict containing the imported names and their counts, sorted from most frequent to least.

### tec.import_counting.modules_imported_under_folder(root)

Generator of imported module (dot path) names

* **Parameters:**
  **root**
* **Returns:**


# _autosummary/tec.imports.html.md

# tec.imports

Find the imports of python code, using the standard library’s `ast`.

This module answers the question  *“what does this code import?”* by parsing the
code into an abstract syntax tree and walking it – so, unlike the regex-based
[`tec.import_counting`](_autosummary/tec.import_counting.html.md#module-tec.import_counting), it is not fooled by import-looking strings, comments,
or line continuations.

The simple thing is simple:

```pycon
>>> [imp.name for imp in imports_in_code("import os\nfrom json import dumps")]
['os', 'json.dumps']
```

The interface has three levels, from most to least specific:

- [`imports_in_code()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.imports_in_code): imports of a string of python code
- [`find_imports()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.find_imports): imports of a single `.py` file
- [`imports_under_folder()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.imports_under_folder) / [`count_imports()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.count_imports): imports of every `.py`
  file under a folder – reached through the `PyFilesReader`
  store, so a “folder” can also be a module object, a package, or the path of an
  `__init__.py` file

[`ModuleImports`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ModuleImports) offers the same information as a `Mapping` from module
dotpath to the imports of that module.

#### NOTE
this module replaces the vendored copy of the (GPL-2.0-or-later) third
party `findimports` project that `tec` used to ship as `tec.findimports`.
It is an independent implementation, written against the standard library, so
that `tec` can be distributed under its own Apache-2.0 terms.

### Module Attributes

| [`CODE_STRING_FILENAME`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.CODE_STRING_FILENAME)             | Placeholder used as the `filename` of imports parsed from a code string.                                                 |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`ABSOLUTE_IMPORT_LEVEL`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ABSOLUTE_IMPORT_LEVEL)            | Value of [`ImportInfo.level`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo.level) for an absolute (non-relative) import.        |
| [`DFLT_IMPORT_KEY`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.DFLT_IMPORT_KEY)(imp)             | Default aggregation key of [`count_imports()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.count_imports): the top-level package name. |
| [`DFLT_PATH_FILT`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.DFLT_PATH_FILT)                   | `None`, i.e. no filtering beyond the store's own restriction to `.py` files.                                             |
| [`DFLT_ON_PARSE_ERROR`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.DFLT_ON_PARSE_ERROR)(error, path) | Default reaction to a file that can't be parsed while walking a folder.                                                  |
| [`FOREIGN_PATH_SEP`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.FOREIGN_PATH_SEP)                 | Path separator that is legal but not native on this platform (`'/'` on Windows, `None` elsewhere).                       |

### Functions

| [`DFLT_IMPORT_KEY`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.DFLT_IMPORT_KEY)(imp)                            | Default aggregation key of [`count_imports()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.count_imports): the top-level package name.   |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`DFLT_ON_PARSE_ERROR`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.DFLT_ON_PARSE_ERROR)(error, path)                | Default reaction to a file that can't be parsed while walking a folder.                                                    |
| [`base_package_of`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.base_package_of)(imp)                            | The top-level package name of an import (`''` for relative imports).                                                       |
| [`count_imports`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.count_imports)(src, \*[, path_filt, ...])        | Count the imports of every `.py` file under `src`.                                                                         |

### tec.imports.ABSOLUTE_IMPORT_LEVEL *= 0*

Value of [`ImportInfo.level`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo.level) for an absolute (non-relative) import.

### tec.imports.CODE_STRING_FILENAME *= '<string>'*

Placeholder used as the `filename` of imports parsed from a code string.

### tec.imports.DFLT_IMPORT_KEY(imp)

Default aggregation key of [`count_imports()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.count_imports): the top-level package name.

* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

### tec.imports.DFLT_ON_PARSE_ERROR(error, path)

Default reaction to a file that can’t be parsed while walking a folder. Folders
of real-world code routinely contain a stray py2 (or templated) file, so the
default is to warn and move on instead of aborting the whole walk.

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

### tec.imports.DFLT_PATH_FILT *= None*

`None`, i.e. no filtering beyond the store’s own
restriction to `.py` files.

* **Type:**
  Default file-path predicate

### tec.imports.FOREIGN_PATH_SEP *= None*

Path separator that is legal but not native on this platform (`'/'` on Windows,
`None` elsewhere). File stores are not required to use the native one.

### *class* tec.imports.ImportInfo(name, filename='<string>', lineno=0, level=0)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

A single imported name, along with where it was found.

```pycon
>>> imp = ImportInfo("os.path", "a.py", 3)
>>> imp.name, imp.lineno, imp.is_relative
('os.path', 3, False)
```

Relative imports carry the number of leading dots in `level`:

```pycon
>>> ImportInfo("sibling", "a.py", 1, level=1).is_relative
True
```

#### filename *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* *= '<string>'*

File the import was found in ([`CODE_STRING_FILENAME`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.CODE_STRING_FILENAME) if unknown).

#### *property* is_relative *: [bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*

True if, and only if, this is a relative (`from .x import y`) import.

#### level *: [int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)* *= 0*

Number of leading dots of a relative import (`0` if absolute).

#### lineno *: [int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)* *= 0*

1-based line number of the `import`/`from` statement.

#### name *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*

Dotted name of what is imported (e.g. `'os.path'`, `'json.dumps'`).

### *class* tec.imports.ModuleImports(src, , root_module_str='')

Bases: `KvReader`

`Mapping` from module dotpath to the tuple of imports of that module.

* **Parameters:**
  * **src** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Anything `PyFilesReader` accepts: a folder path,
    a module or package object, or the path of an `__init__.py` file.
  * **root_module_str** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Prefix to give the module dotpaths (the keys).

#### NOTE
the dotpath-to-file index is computed once, lazily, on first use – files
added to the folder afterwards will not show up in an existing instance.

```pycon
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
...     _ = Path(root, '__init__.py').write_text('')
...     _ = Path(root, 'a.py').write_text('import os\nfrom json import dumps\n')
...     s = ModuleImports(root, root_module_str='pkg')
...     keys, n = sorted(s), len(s)
...     names = [imp.name for imp in s['pkg.a']]
>>> keys
['pkg.__init__', 'pkg.a']
>>> n
2
>>> names
['os', 'json.dumps']
```

### tec.imports.base_package_of(imp)

The top-level package name of an import (`''` for relative imports).

```pycon
>>> base_package_of("collections.abc")
'collections'
>>> base_package_of(ImportInfo("os.path"))
'os'
```

A relative import has no resolvable top-level package, so it maps to `''`:

```pycon
>>> base_package_of(ImportInfo("sibling", level=1))
''
```

* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

### tec.imports.count_imports(src, \*, path_filt=None, import_key=<function base_package_of>, on_parse_error=<function warn_of_parse_error>)

Count the imports of every `.py` file under `src`.

* **Parameters:**
  * **src** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Anything `PyFilesReader` accepts (see
    [`imports_under_folder()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.imports_under_folder)).
  * **path_filt** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)], [`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)]]) – Optional predicate on the store’s (relative) file paths.
  * **import_key** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[[`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo)], [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]) – What to count: applied to each [`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo), it
    returns the value that is tallied. Defaults to [`base_package_of()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.base_package_of),
    i.e. the top-level package name.
  * **on_parse_error** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[[`SyntaxError`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#SyntaxError), [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)], [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)]) – See [`imports_under_folder()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.imports_under_folder).
* **Return type:**
  [`Counter`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.Counter)
* **Returns:**
  A [`collections.Counter`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.Counter).

```pycon
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
...     _ = Path(root, 'a.py').write_text('import os\nfrom os import path\n')
...     _ = Path(root, 'b.py').write_text('import os.path\nimport json\n')
...     counts = count_imports(root)
...     full = count_imports(root, import_key=lambda imp: imp.name)
>>> sorted(counts.items())
[('json', 1), ('os', 3)]
>>> sorted(full.items())
[('json', 1), ('os', 1), ('os.path', 2)]
```

### tec.imports.find_imports(filename)

Generate the [`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo) of every import of the `.py` file `filename`.

* **Parameters:**
  **filename** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Path of the python file to parse.
* **Return type:**
  [`Iterator`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Iterator)[[`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo)]
* **Returns:**
  A generator of [`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo).

```pycon
>>> imports = list(find_imports(__file__))
>>> "ast" in {imp.name for imp in imports}
True
>>> {imp.filename for imp in imports} == {__file__}
True
```

### tec.imports.ignore_parse_error(error, path)

`on_parse_error` strategy: silently skip the file.

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

### tec.imports.imports_in_code(code, , filename='<string>')

Generate the [`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo) of every import found in `code`.

* **Parameters:**
  * **code** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The python source to parse.
  * **filename** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – What to record as the origin of the imports found.
* **Return type:**
  [`Iterator`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Iterator)[[`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo)]
* **Returns:**
  A generator of [`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo).

```pycon
>>> code = '''
... import os, sys
... import os.path as osp
... from collections.abc import Mapping
... from . import sibling
... from ..pkg import thing
... '''
>>> [imp.name for imp in imports_in_code(code)]
['os', 'sys', 'os.path', 'collections.abc.Mapping', 'sibling', 'pkg.thing']
```

Unlike a regex-based scan, text that merely *looks* like an import is ignored:

```pycon
>>> list(imports_in_code('x = "import antigravity"  # import antigravity'))
[]
```

Imports nested in functions, classes, `try` blocks etc. are included:

```pycon
>>> [imp.name for imp in imports_in_code("def f():\n    import lazily\n")]
['lazily']
```

Code that doesn’t parse raises a `SyntaxError` naming the offending file:

```pycon
>>> list(imports_in_code("import ;", filename="broken.py")
... )
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
SyntaxError: invalid syntax (broken.py, line 1)
```

### tec.imports.imports_under_folder(src, \*, path_filt=None, on_parse_error=<function warn_of_parse_error>)

Generate the [`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo) of every `.py` file under `src`.

* **Parameters:**
  * **src** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Anything `PyFilesReader` accepts: a folder path,
    a module or package object, or the path of an `__init__.py` file.
  * **path_filt** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)], [`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)]]) – Optional predicate on the store’s (relative) file paths, to
    narrow down the files that are parsed. `None` means “all `.py` files”.
  * **on_parse_error** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[[`SyntaxError`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#SyntaxError), [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)], [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)]) – What to do with a file that doesn’t parse. Called with
    the `SyntaxError` and the path. See [`raise_parse_error()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.raise_parse_error),
    [`warn_of_parse_error()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.warn_of_parse_error) (the default) and [`ignore_parse_error()`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ignore_parse_error).
* **Return type:**
  [`Iterator`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Iterator)[[`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo)]
* **Returns:**
  A generator of [`ImportInfo`](_autosummary/tec.imports.html.md#tec.imports.ImportInfo).

```pycon
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
...     _ = Path(root, 'a.py').write_text('import os\n')
...     _ = Path(root, 'b_test.py').write_text('import json\n')
...     all_names = sorted(imp.name for imp in imports_under_folder(root))
...     kept = sorted(
...         imp.name
...         for imp in imports_under_folder(
...             root, path_filt=lambda p: not p.endswith('_test.py')
...         )
...     )
>>> all_names
['json', 'os']
>>> kept
['os']
```

### tec.imports.raise_parse_error(error, path)

`on_parse_error` strategy: let the `SyntaxError` propagate.

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

### tec.imports.warn_of_parse_error(error, path)

`on_parse_error` strategy: warn about the file, then skip it.

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

utilities are importable and so pytest can collect the package without an
import-file-mismatch collision.

### tec.misc.infos_of_packages_under_rootdir(rootdir)

Yields information about packages found recursively under rootdir

> ### Examples

> ```python
>     from collections import defaultdict
>     from operator import itemgetter
>     rootdir = 'PROJECTS_ROOT_DIR'

>     project_info_for_group = defaultdict(list)
>     for group, *info in infos_of_packages_under_rootdir(rootdir):
>          project_info_for_group[group].append(info)

>     for group, projects in project_info_for_group.items():
>         print(f"----- {group} ---------")
>         for project_name, description, readme in projects:
>             one_line_description = description.replace('
> ', ' ')
>             print(f"{project_name}: {one_line_description}")
> ```

|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### tec.misc.manage_pth_file.DFLT_FILENAME_FILT()

x._\_contains_\_(y) <==> y in x.

### tec.misc.manage_pth_file.add_missing_lines(target, source=())

Append the `source` lines missing from `target` to the `target` file.

`target` is a filepath: the missing lines are appended to it in place, and
the list of lines that were added is returned.

```pycon
>>> import os, tempfile
>>> path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), 'lines.txt')
>>> _ = open(path, 'w').write('one\ntwo\n\nthree')
>>> add_missing_lines(path, ['four', '', 'five'])
['four', 'five']
>>> print(open(path).read())
one
two

three
four
five
```

### tec.misc.manage_pth_file.add_to_pth_file(lines, pth_filepath=None)

Add some paths to the pth file (if they’re not there already)

* **Parameters:**
  **lines** – A ; or newline separated string of paths, or a filepath to a file containing these (one per line).

### tec.misc.manage_pth_file.mk_reclone_string(rootdir, save_in_filepath=None, filt=None)

Makes a file with a bunch of reclone instructions.
If `save_in_filepath` is given, it will save to that file.
You are to then chmod 744 the file and run it.

* **Parameters:**
  * **rootdir** – Directory within which to look for package folders
  * **save_in_filepath** – Save to this file
  * **filt** – Function to filter in package folder paths found in rootdir

### tec.misc.manage_pth_file.target_and_missing_items(target, source=())

Add source lines to target lines

```pycon
>>> target_and_missing_items(['one', 'two', '', 'three'], ['four', '', 'five'])
(['one', 'two', '', 'three'], ['four', 'five'])
```

### *class* tec.modules.ModulesReader(module_src, root_module_str='')

Bases: `Store`

By store we mean key-value store. This could be files in a filesystem, objects in s3, or a database. Where and
how the content is stored should be specified, but StoreInterface offers a dict-like interface to this.

```default
__getitem__ calls: _id_of_key                                       _obj_of_data
__setitem__ calls: _id_of_key                   _data_of_obj
__delitem__ calls: _id_of_key
__iter__    calls:                  _key_of_id
```

```pycon
>>> # Default store: no key or value conversion #####################################
>>> from dol import Store
>>> s = Store()
>>> s['foo'] = 33
>>> s['bar'] = 65
>>> assert list(s.items()) == [('foo', 33), ('bar', 65)]
>>> assert list(s.store.items()) == [('foo', 33), ('bar', 65)]  # see that the store contains the same thing
>>>
>>> #################################################################################
>>> # Now let's make stores that have a key and value conversion layer ##############
>>> # input keys will be upper cased, and output keys lower cased ###################
>>> # input values (assumed int) will be converted to ascii string, and visa versa ##
>>> #################################################################################
>>>
>>> def test_store(s):
...     s['foo'] = 33  # write 33 to 'foo'
...     assert 'foo' in s  # __contains__ works
...     assert 'no_such_key' not in s  # __nin__ works
...     s['bar'] = 65  # write 65 to 'bar'
...     assert len(s) == 2  # there are indeed two elements
...     assert list(s) == ['foo', 'bar']  # these are the keys
...     assert list(s.keys()) == ['foo', 'bar']  # the keys() method works!
...     assert list(s.values()) == [33, 65]  # the values() method works!
...     assert list(s.items()) == [('foo', 33), ('bar', 65)]  # these are the items
...     assert list(s.store.items()) == [('FOO', '!'), ('BAR', 'A')]  # but note the internal representation
...     assert s.get('foo') == 33  # the get method works
...     assert s.get('no_such_key', 'something') == 'something'  # return a default value
...     del(s['foo'])  # you can delete an item given its key
...     assert len(s) == 1  # see, only one item left!
...     assert list(s.items()) == [('bar', 65)]  # here it is
>>>
>>> # We can introduce this conversion layer in several ways. Here's a few... ######################
>>> # by subclassing ###############################################################################
>>> class MyStore(Store):
...     def _id_of_key(self, k):
...         return k.upper()
...     def _key_of_id(self, _id):
...         return _id.lower()
...     def _data_of_obj(self, obj):
...         return chr(obj)
...     def _obj_of_data(self, data):
...         return ord(data)
>>> s = MyStore(store=dict())  # note that you don't need to specify dict(), since it's the default
>>> test_store(s)
>>>
>>> # by assigning functions to converters ##########################################################
>>> class MyStore(Store):
...     def __init__(self, store, _id_of_key, _key_of_id, _data_of_obj, _obj_of_data):
...         super().__init__(store)
...         self._id_of_key = _id_of_key
...         self._key_of_id = _key_of_id
...         self._data_of_obj = _data_of_obj
...         self._obj_of_data = _obj_of_data
...
>>> s = MyStore(dict(),
...             _id_of_key=lambda k: k.upper(),
...             _key_of_id=lambda _id: _id.lower(),
...             _data_of_obj=lambda obj: chr(obj),
...             _obj_of_data=lambda data: ord(data))
>>> test_store(s)
>>>
>>> # using a Mixin class #############################################################################
>>> class Mixin:
...     def _id_of_key(self, k):
...         return k.upper()
...     def _key_of_id(self, _id):
...         return _id.lower()
...     def _data_of_obj(self, obj):
...         return chr(obj)
...     def _obj_of_data(self, data):
...         return ord(data)
...
>>> class MyStore(Mixin, Store):  # note that the Mixin must come before Store in the mro
...     pass
...
>>> s = MyStore()  # no dict()? No, because default anyway
>>> test_store(s)
>>>
>>> # adding wrapper methods to an already made Store instance #########################################
>>> s = Store(dict())
>>> s._id_of_key=lambda k: k.upper()
>>> s._key_of_id=lambda _id: _id.lower()
>>> s._data_of_obj=lambda obj: chr(obj)
>>> s._obj_of_data=lambda data: ord(data)
>>> test_store(s)
```

Note on defining your own “Mapping Views”.

When you do a `.keys()`, a `.values()` or `.items()` you’re getting a `MappingView`
instance; an iterable and sized container that provides some methods to access
particular aspects of the wrapped mapping.

If you need to customize the behavior of these instances, you should avoid
overriding the `keys`, `values` or `items` methods directly, but instead
override the `KeysView`, `ValuesView` or `ItemsView` classes that they use.

For more, see: [https://github.com/i2mint/dol/wiki/Mapping-Views](https://github.com/i2mint/dol/wiki/Mapping-Views)

# _autosummary/tec.packages.html.md

# tec.packages

A few functions to investigate what objects can be imported from a module
(and the depth of the dot-path to import those objects directly).

The main function, print_top_level_diagnosis,
prints a diagnosis of the imports that can be optained from the (top level) module.
That is, those objects that can by imported by doing:

```text
from module import obj
```

though the object’s code may be several package levels down (say module.sub1.sub2.obj).

```text
>> import numpy, pandas, scipy
>> print_top_level_diagnosis(numpy)
--------- numpy ---------
601 objects can be imported from top level numpy:
  20 modules
  300 functions
  104 types

depth   count
0       163
1       406
2       2
3       29
4       1

>> print_top_level_diagnosis(pandas)
--------- pandas ---------
115 objects can be imported from top level pandas:
  12 modules
  55 functions
  40 types

depth   count
0       12
3       37
4       65
5       1

>> print_top_level_diagnosis(scipy)
--------- scipy ---------
582 objects can be imported from top level scipy:
  9 modules
  412 functions
  96 types

depth   count
0       61
1       395
2       4
3       122
```

### tec.peek.print_signature(func, sep='\\n', prefix='', suffix='')

Print the signature of a callable

* **Parameters:**
  * **func** – Callable to print the signature of
  * **sep** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) | [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)) – If None, will print the signature as inspect.signature would.
    If a string, will use the string to separate the parameter specifications

```pycon
>>> print_signature(print_signature)
func
sep: str | None = '\n'
prefix: str = ''
suffix: str = ''
>>> print_signature(print_signature, None)
(func, sep: str | None = '\n', prefix: str = '', suffix: str = '')
>>> print_signature(print_signature, '\n * ', prefix=' * ', suffix='\n')
 * func
 * sep: str | None = '\n'
 * prefix: str = ''
 * suffix: str = ''
```

### tec.peek.print_source(o, start=None, end=None, doc=True)

Prints the source code of the input object. Can specify lines to print with start and end.

```pycon
>>> print_source(print_source, 0, 1)
def print_source(o, start=None, end=None, doc=True):

>>> print_source(print_source, 11)
    _lines, _ = getsourcelines(o)
    print(''.join(_lines[slice(start, end)]))
```

### tec.pip_packaging.format_str_vals_of_dict(d, , max_formatting_loops=10, \*\*kwargs)

* **Parameters:**
  * **d**
  * **max_formatting_loops**
  * **kwargs**
* **Returns:**

```pycon
>>> d = {
...     'filepath': '{root}/{file}.{ext}',
...     'ext': 'txt'
... }
>>> format_str_vals_of_dict(d, root='ROOT', file='FILE')
{'filepath': 'ROOT/FILE.txt', 'ext': 'txt'}
```

Note that if the input mapping `d` and the kwargs have a conflict, the mapping version is used!

```pycon
>>> format_str_vals_of_dict(d, root='ROOT', file='FILE', ext='will_not_be_used')
{'filepath': 'ROOT/FILE.txt', 'ext': 'txt'}
```

But if you want to override an input mapping, you can – the usual way:

```pycon
>>> format_str_vals_of_dict(dict(d, ext='will_be_used'), root='ROOT', file='FILE')
{'filepath': 'ROOT/FILE.will_be_used', 'ext': 'will_be_used'}
```

If you don’t provide enough fields to satisfy all the format fields in the values of `d`,
you’ll be told to bugger off.

```pycon
>>> format_str_vals_of_dict(d, root='ROOT')
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: I won't be able to complete that. You'll need to provide the values for:
  file
```

And it’s recursive…

```pycon
>>> d = {
...     'filepath': '{root}/{filename}',
...     'filename': '{file}.{ext}'
... }
>>> my_configs = {'root': 'ROOT', 'file': 'FILE', 'ext': 'EXT'}
>>> format_str_vals_of_dict(d, **my_configs)
{'filepath': 'ROOT/FILE.EXT', 'filename': 'FILE.EXT'}
```

# TODO: Could make the above work if filename is give, but not file nor ext! At least as an option.

> get_version('tec')

### tec.pip_packaging.ujoin(\*args)

Join strings with the url seperator (/).

Note that will add a / where it’s missing (as in between ‘[https://pypi.org](https://pypi.org)’ and ‘project/’),
and only use one if two consecutive tokens use respectively end and start with a /
(as in ‘project/’ and ‘/pipoke/’).

```pycon
>>> ujoin('https://pypi.org', 'project/', '/pipoke/')
'https://pypi.org/project/pipoke/'
```

Extremal cases

```pycon
>>> ujoin('https://pypi.org')
'https://pypi.org'
>>> ujoin('https://pypi.org/')
'https://pypi.org/'
>>> ujoin('')
''
>>> ujoin()
''
```

### tec.snake_food_import_counting.base_module_imports_in_module_recursive(module)

Get a list of strings showing what base modules that are imported in a module, recursively.
It’s the recursive version of the base_modules_used_in_module function.
Recursive in the sense that if module is a package module (i.e. containing a \_\_init_\_.py and further submodules),
the base_modules_used_in_module function will be applied to all .py files under the mother folder.
Function returns a count (Counter object) of the number of modules where each base module was found.

* **Parameters:**
  * **module** – An actual module object the file of the module (as given by inspect.getfile(module)
  * **module_names** – Modules to filter for.
    None: Will grab all modules
    A list or tuple: Of modules to grab
    If not will assume module_names is a regex to apply to find module names
* **Returns:**

### tec.snake_food_import_counting.base_modules_used_in_module(module)

Get a list of strings showing what base modules that are imported in a module.

* **Parameters:**

### tec.stores.py_files_with_contents_matching_pattern(files_src, pattern)

Yields (relative) file paths of .py files whose contents match pattern.

* **Parameters:**
  * **files_src** – Source of files. Module, package, folder, or \_\_init_\_.py file.
  * **pattern** – regular expression (string or re.Pattern object)

Let’s see what modules of asyncio contain the “import io” string:

```pycon
>>> import asyncio
>>> set(py_files_with_contents_matching_pattern(asyncio, 'import io')).issuperset(
...     {'proactor_events.py', 'unix_events.py'})
True
```

### tec.util.bitmap_selection(iterable, selector)

Select items of an iterable with items of a selector sequence of the same size.
The selector items should be, or resolve to, a `bool`.

```pycon
>>> list(bitmap_selection([2, 4, 6, 8], [True, False, True, False]))
[2, 6]
>>> tuple(bitmap_selection(range(5), [1, 0, None, '', 'blah']))
(0, 4)
```

### tec.util.find(query, items, query_matches_item=<built-in function eq>, query_key=<function identity>, item_key=<function identity>)

Find anything in an iterable of items, based on your query language of choice.

Is limited to no query or items type. All you need to do is define what a match
of a query and item is, through the `query_matches_item` function.

Example use:

```pycon
>>> items = [
...     'www.google.com',
...     'www.yahoo.com',
...     'www.harvard.edu',
...     'web.mit.edu',
... ]
>>> list(find('www.harvard.edu', items))
['www.harvard.edu']
>>> list(find('oo', items, query_matches_item=lambda q, i: q in i))
['www.google.com', 'www.yahoo.com']
>>> list(find('edu', items, item_key=lambda item: item.split('.')[-1]))
['www.harvard.edu', 'web.mit.edu']
```

Often you may want to use functools.partials to make a searcher you can reuse
without having to specify the particulars of the search (including or not the
items you want to search).

```pycon
>>> from functools import partial
>>> finder = partial(find, items=items, query_matches_item=lambda q, i: q in i,
...                    query_key=str.lower, item_key=str.lower)
>>> list(finder('GOOGLE'))
['www.google.com']
```

Note that the `query_matches_item` is sufficient.
For example, in the above we could have done it like this:

```pycon
>>> list(find('GOOGLE', items, lambda q, i: q.lower() in i.lower()))
['www.google.com']
```

There’s never any actual need for the key functions, but they’re provided for
convenience and reuse of general `query_matches_item` functions.

### tec.util.find_objects(pattern, objects, objects_to_strings=<function \_if_not_iterable_get_attributes>, \*, key=None)

Find strings matching a given pattern, possibly sorting them in a specific way.

* **Parameters:**
  * **pattern** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The pattern to search (string representing a regular expression).
  * **objects** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – An iterable of strings or an object that will resolve in one.
  * **objects_to_strings** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[[`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)], [`Iterable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Iterable)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]]) – The function that resolves the `objects` input
    (which is not even necessarily an iterable) into an iterable of strings.
  * **key** – If not None, will be used to sort matched objects.
    `key` will be applied to objects of type `re.Match`;
    see [https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html#match-objects](https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html#match-objects) to get an idea of
    how to define the right key function.
    If `key` is an iterable (“of callables”, assumed), make an
    aggregate of these functions that will return a tuple of the sort keys.
    This is akin to sorting by one columns primarly, a second secondarily, etc.
* **Returns:**
  A generator of matched strings.

```pycon
>>> kwargs = dict(
...     pattern='li',
...     objects='bob and lilabet like to play with alice',
...     objects_to_strings=str.split,
... )
>>> list(find_objects(**kwargs))
['lilabet', 'like', 'alice']
```

Sort the results in reverse length of string:

```pycon
>>> list(find_objects(**kwargs, key=lambda x: -len(x.string)))
['lilabet', 'alice', 'like']
```

Sort the results according to how early in the string the match happens:

```pycon
>>> from operator import methodcaller
>>> list(find_objects(**kwargs, key=methodcaller('span')))
['lilabet', 'like', 'alice']
```

The same as above, but with secondary “length” sorting:

```pycon
>>> tuple(  # for a change!
...     find_objects(**kwargs, key=[methodcaller('span'), lambda x: len(x.string)])
... )
('like', 'lilabet', 'alice')
```

### tec.util.func_fanout(\*args, funcs, \*\*kwargs)

Util to make a function that applies multiple functions to a single input.
Note that the function returns a generator that needs to be “consumed” to actually
get the outputs of the function.

`func_fanout` is meant to be used with `functools.partial` to “make” the
desired function, such as:

```pycon
>>> from functools import partial
>>> f = partial(func_fanout, funcs=[
...     lambda x, y: x + y,
...     lambda x, y: x * y,
... ])
>>> list(f(2, 3))
[5, 6]
>>> tuple(f(3, y=4))
(7, 12)
```

<!-- seealso: ``i2.multi_object.FuncFanout`` for a more involved version of this. -->

### tec.util.import_and_add_if_available(obj_name, module_name, as_name=None, scope=None, if_already_in_scope=None, if_not_found=None)

Import object named `obj_name` from module named `module_name`, sticking it
in scope (a dict, usually locals()).

* **Parameters:**
  * **scope** ([`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)) – A dict where the object will be stored (if found). Usually locals().
  * **obj_name** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The name of the object to import
  * **module_name** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The name of the module to import the object from
  * **as_name** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) | [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)) – The name to use in the scope. Defaults to `obj_name`
  * **if_already_in_scope** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable) | [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)) – If not None, should be a `(scope, as_name, obj)`
    callable that will provide the return value if `as_name` is already in the
    scope.
    This is to be able to overwrite the default of simply doing a
    `scope[as_name] = obj` (having the net effect of resolving name conflicts
    by a “last one seen wins” strategy.
  * **if_not_found** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable) | [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)) – If not None, should be a `(obj_name, module_name)` callable
    that will provide the return value if `obj_name` is not found in
    `module_name`.
* **Returns:**

```pycon
>>> from functools import partial  # not necessary, but represents use case
>>> scope = dict()  # you'd usually put locals() here
>>> acquire = partial(import_and_add_if_available, scope=scope)
>>> acquire('join', 'os.path')
True
>>> acquire('isfile', 'os.path', as_name='check_if_file_exists')
True
>>> acquire('not_in_os_path', 'os.path')  # returns False: not found in os.path
False
>>> acquire('object', 'does.not.exist')  # returns None: the module_name not found
>>> import os
>>> assert (scope ==
...     {'join': os.path.join, 'check_if_file_exists': os.path.isfile}
... )
```

See in the above that neither `'not_in_os_path'` nor `'object'` are in
`scope`. They were simply skipped.

### tec.util.name_and_object_pairs(objects, objects_to_iterable=<function \_attribute_name_object_pairs>, \*, name_filt=<function \_not_prefixed_by_underscore>, obj_filt=<built-in function callable>, name_of_obj=operator.attrgetter('_\_name_\_'))

Get (name, object) pairs from source of objects

* **Parameters:**
  * **objects** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – The source we want to extract name and object pairs from.
    Could be an explicit list of pairs, or a single object (like a module)
    from which we’ll generate these (using `objects_to_iterable`)
  * **objects_to_iterable** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[`...`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#Ellipsis), [`Iterable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Iterable)]) – If the input `objects` isn’t already an iterable,
    the function to make it so
  * **name_filt** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[`...`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#Ellipsis), [`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)]) – A condition on the name
  * **obj_filt** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[`...`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#Ellipsis), [`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)]) – A condition on the object
  * **name_of_obj** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)[[[`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)], [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – when an element of the iterable isn’t a (name, obj) pair,
    the function to get the name of a the object.

Get method names of the dict class:

```pycon
>>> next(zip(*name_and_object_pairs(dict)))
('clear', 'copy', 'fromkeys', 'get', 'items', 'keys', 'pop', 'popitem', 'setdefault', 'update', 'values')
```

Get only those names of dict methods that contain the string ‘keys’:

```pycon
>>> next(zip(*name_and_object_pairs(dict, name_filt=lambda x: 'keys' in x)))
('fromkeys', 'keys')
```

Prints information on callable attributes of obj (module, class, …)
